newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia will have to wait for cheap phone calls.
newsitem.headline: Australia will have to wait for cheap phone calls.

text.p: The long-awaited deregulation of Australia's telecommunications industry becomes reality next week, but users will have to wait a while longer to reap the benefits of the new era.
Although both local and international call rates will eventually be pushed down by deregulation, there has been no flurry of international competitors queueing up to break into the Australian market.
With telecoms markets opening up around the world, analysts suggested there were better returns to be had elsewhere.
Paul Buddie, an independent telecoms analyst, said of the deregulation: "After July 1st you will get more competition and prices will fall."
Analysts say local call charges, which are on an untimed basis, are expected to fall from a current level of 25 cents to as low as 15 cents, a drop of up to 40 percent.
But not yet.

With only a couple of days to go until the last shackles are lifted, there has been little sign that call charges will soon fall. There have been no major advertising campaigns by either existing players or new entrants promising cheaper calls.
"The fact that we haven't seen a flood of advertising indicates that there won't be an immediate big change," said Mark Smeaton, telecommunications analyst at Macquarie Equities.
"If any big players were going to come in a big way then they would already have been around," Smeaton said.
Telecom markets are opening up all around the world, encouraged by the telecoms free-trade agreement reached in February under World Trade Organisation auspices.
"There are opportunities all over the place and they may well be better than Australia," said Brian Perkins, chairman of telecoms industry group SPAN.

Deregulation also comes at a time when Australia's two biggest telephone carriers state-owned Telstra Corp Ltd and Optus Communications Pty Ltd are sorting themselves out ahead of their respective forthcoming sharemarket floats.

Australia's A$25 billion telecom market is dominated by former monopoly Telstra, which still holds a tight grip on the local-call market, but has lost sizeable market share in the long-distance market in the past five years.

However, Telstra is still likely to increase its business as the local telecom market is forecast to grow by 10 percent a year for the foreseeable future, boosted by new telephony service and the mobile phone market, analysts said.
About 25 percent of Australians have mobile phones -- one of the highest penetration rates in the world.

Deregulation puts the Australian government in a delicate situation as it wants to encourage open competition, but also to maximise proceeds from its planned sale of a third of its holding in Telstra later this year.

"In theory it could be very difficult for the government, but I think the government is probably more interested in competitive issues than maximising the value of Telstra," said one Sydney-based telecommunications analyst.

Telstra and Optus are both exposed to the pay TV industry, which has lost nearly A$2 billion. Analysts have tipped a pay TV settlement to stem the losses from pay TV and appease investor discontent ahead of the public floats of both groups.

The float of Optus has already delayed due to its involvement in pay TV. Optus has also been plagued by technical problems with its local telephony service since its launch a year ago. The telephony service is delivered on the same cable as its pay TV service Optus Vision.

The Australian government, which owns all of Telstra is planning to sell a third of its stake through a public share offer later this year, which could raise a minimum of A$8 billion, making it Australia's largest share offer.

The float of Optus, which is backed by Cable and Wireless Plc of Britain and BellSouth Corp of the U.S., looks likely to be in 1998 after a recent management changes and the integration of Optus Vision after a merger in April.
Under Australia's new telecommunications regime, the number of carrier licences issued will not be limited and there will be no restrictions on the services they provide.

AAPT Telecommunications Pty Ltd, which is partly owned by Singapore Telecommunications Ltd, is seen as one of the frontrunners to get a carrier licence with further licences seen going to existing service providers.

Service providers have welcomed the recommendation from the new industry regulator the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) which ruled a cut to interconnect fees of up to 35 percent to Telstra's main network from July 1.

Australian started to deregulate its telecoms market in 1992, which the entry of Optus as a rival carrier to Telstra in the long distance and mobile markets, and cellular phone specialist Vodafone Plc in the mobile market.
